prime.problem: Some payoffs depend on the whole path (an average of 12 monthly closes) or on many assets. They have no closed form, and a tree can't track them because it stops recombining. You need a method that prices any payoff you can compute from a simulated path, and a way to know how wrong its answer is.
prime.fits: Third card of the pricing part. It computes the same discounted Q-average as the binomial and Black–Scholes cards, but by sampling GBM paths (the GBM card) at drift r. Its error bar is the CLT from cs-9.
expect: the estimator e<sup>−rT</sup> · mean of payoffs
prime.goal: Price the shared call by simulation with an honest error bar, cut the error with antithetic and control variates, and say when simulation is the right tool and when it isn't.

attend: Why must the simulated stock grow at r − σ²/2 in the log, not at the real-world μ?
Why does the error fall like 1/√n, and what does that cost per extra correct digit?
Why does pairing Z with −Z help a call but could hurt a payoff that is symmetric in Z?
Why does the geometric Asian make such a strong control for the arithmetic one (÷ 1,281)?
Why does Monte Carlo struggle with American exercise and with bumped Greeks?

must: Price = e<sup>−rT</sup>E<sub>Q</sub>[payoff] → simulate S<sub>T</sub> under Q (log drift r − σ²/2) → average the discounted payoffs → the law of large numbers makes the average converge to the price
Independent payoffs with sd s → the average's error is s/√n (CLT) → 10× the paths buys only √10 ≈ 3.16× less error → one more digit costs 100× the paths → so reduce s instead of raising n

Antithetic pairs (Z, −Z) → for a payoff monotone in Z, a high payoff meets a low one → the pair's average has less variance (÷ 2.00 for the call) → but a payoff symmetric in Z gets positively correlated pairs → variance can rise

A control variate with a known mean, simulated on the same paths → subtract b × (its error) → the closer it tracks the target, the more variance cancels → geometric Asian (exact 5.9402) vs arithmetic Asian: ÷ 1,281
elevated: Error ∝ 1/√n regardless of dimension → trees and PDE grids grow exponentially with each extra asset or path variable → Monte Carlo is the only method whose cost doesn't explode with dimension, which is its whole selling point

compress.prompt: Write the estimator and its error bar from memory, then list the two ways to shrink the error bar (more n, smaller s) and one technique for each part of s you can cut. One sentence on when you'd not use Monte Carlo.
checklist: simulate under Q with log drift r − σ²/2, discount the average payoff
SE = s/√n, and a 95% interval is ±1.96 SE
antithetic pairs and control variates cut s
use it for path-dependent or high-dimensional payoffs; not for a plain European (closed form) or American exercise (tree)

retrieve.q: Explain why a Monte Carlo price for a stock option uses r in the simulated drift even if you're confident the stock will grow at 8%.
answer: the price is the cost of the hedge, which is an expectation under Q
under Q the stock earns r, so paths must be simulated at r (log drift r − σ²/2)
using μ would give the expected payoff to a holder, not a no-arbitrage price, and would be too high

retrieve.q: Walk through how many paths you'd need for a standard error of 0.001 on the shared call, with and without the e<sup>−rT</sup>S<sub>T</sub> control variate.
answer: the control variate divides the variance by 6.89, so ≈ 3.1 × 10⁷ paths
either way, far more than the 10⁶ that take about 0.25 s

retrieve.q: A colleague prices a European call with 10⁶ paths and reports 10.4697 ± 0.0147. What would you tell them, and when would their approach be the right one?
answer: Black–Scholes gives 10.4506 exactly in O(1); simulation adds noise for nothing here
their interval contains the true price, so the estimate isn't wrong, just wasteful
simulation is right for path-dependent (Asian, barrier, lookback) or many-asset payoffs

compare.q: The tree works backwards and Monte Carlo works forwards. Which payoffs does each handle naturally, and what is each method's error law?
answer: tree: backward induction, so it knows the value of holding at each node and handles early exercise; error ∝ 1/N
Monte Carlo: forward paths, so it handles any path-dependent payoff; error ∝ 1/√n
the tree fails when payoffs depend on the path (no recombination); MC fails at early exercise and gets expensive for high precision

compare.q: Where exactly does the CLT enter the Monte Carlo card, and what assumption would break the ±1.96 SE interval?
answer: the sample mean of n independent payoffs is approximately normal with sd s/√n
that's what justifies reading ±1.96 SE as a 95% interval
it needs independent paths and finite payoff variance; heavy-tailed payoffs or a bad random generator break it

predict.q: Price a straddle (payoff |S<sub>T</sub> − 100|) on the shared contract with 10⁶ payoffs. Will antithetic pairs reduce its variance as they did for the call, do nothing, or make it worse? Commit before revealing.
predict.answer: Worse. Near the money a straddle pays for moves in either direction, so Z and −Z tend to give similar payoffs: the pair is positively correlated. In a seed-0 run (500,000 pairs vs 10⁶ plain payoffs) the variance ratio is 0.61, meaning antithetic variates increased the variance by about 1.6×. For comparison, the ratio was 2.0 for the call and 25 for the linear forward S<sub>T</sub> − 100, where the pairing cancels almost everything. Antithetics help when the payoff is monotone in Z.

apply.task: Modify the card's code to price three payoffs on the shared contract with 10⁶ plain payoffs and with 500,000 antithetic pairs (seed 0): the call, the straddle |S<sub>T</sub> − 100|, and the forward S<sub>T</sub> − 100. Report estimate, SE and the variance ratio. Check the straddle against Black–Scholes C + P.
apply.done: Call ≈ 10.4697, ratio ≈ 2.0; straddle ≈ 16.04 against C + P = 16.0241, ratio ≈ 0.61; forward ≈ 4.90 against S − Ke<sup>−rT</sup> = 4.8771, ratio ≈ 25. You can explain each ratio from the payoff's shape in Z.
apply.hint: The ratio is plain variance ÷ (2 × variance of the pair averages), so it compares the same number of payoff evaluations.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: did you expect antithetics to always help?
Could you explain 1/√n to someone without saying "CLT"?
Which link is still fuzzy: simulate under Q → price, or correlation between pairs → variance reduction?
When would you choose a tree, the formula or simulation for a new payoff, and what question decides it?
What will you revisit before the checkpoint: the three pricing methods' error laws side by side?
